paragraphs: Radar semantic segmentation assigns meaningful categories to radar measurements. PeakConv was designed to retain the prominent signal peaks that help distinguish targets while using convolutional processing. Its fixed sampling rule, however, makes it harder to handle targets whose responses spread differently across frequencies, as well as noise and clutter that vary across locations and over time.

The paper introduces AdaPKC, which replaces the preset peak receptive field with an adaptive one. The central change concerns which surrounding signal information the convolution uses when processing a peak. Allowing that receptive field to adapt addresses the mismatch between a fixed sampling pattern and changing radar responses. The authors also introduce a fine-tuning technique intended to further improve segmentation networks built with AdaPKC.

Experiments use real radar measurements, including a public low-cost millimeter-wave driving dataset and a collected Ku-band surveillance dataset. The authors report that AdaPKC-based models outperform other state-of-the-art methods on the evaluated segmentation tasks. These findings support adapting peak processing to the characteristics of radar signals across the tested settings.
neurips-2024-adapkc-peakconv-with-adapti.tldr: AdaPKC adapts how radar convolutions sample around signal peaks, improving semantic segmentation on evaluated real radar datasets.

paragraphs: A scene graph describes objects in an image and the relationships between them. Learning these graphs continuously is challenging because new scenes can require a model to add relationships, revise existing ones, and retain earlier knowledge. The surrounding context also affects how objects relate, making adaptation more involved than recognizing individual objects alone.

The paper establishes a benchmark for continual scene graph generation with three regimes: relationship incremental learning, scene incremental learning, and relationship generalization. It also proposes RAS, a replay method that breaks scene graphs into components and recombines them. Those recomposed graphs guide the synthesis of scenes, which the model revisits to practice its scene-understanding abilities across familiar and unfamiliar environments.

The experiments show that combining existing continual-learning methods with scene-graph models presents substantial difficulties. RAS improves continual scene graph generation efficiency while addressing privacy and memory usage, according to the reported results. Its contribution is to make compositional scene structure part of the replay process, so retained knowledge can be exercised through synthesized scenes.
neurips-2024-adaptive-visual-scene-under.tldr: RAS replays synthesized scenes built from recomposed scene graphs to support continual learning of objects and relationships.

paragraphs: A policy learned from a few demonstrations can behave inconsistently with what those demonstrations intended. This paper defines Adaptable Error Detection as recognizing such behavior from visual observations in new environments. The detector must work online, meaning it cannot wait to see the entire rollout, and some errors may produce only subtle visible changes.

To study these challenges together, the authors create a benchmark containing 322 base environments and 153 novel environments. They introduce Pattern Observer, or PrObe, which extracts patterns from the policy's internal feature representations. Its learning objectives help distinguish representations associated with normal behavior from those associated with errors, supporting detection beyond conspicuous changes in the observed scene.

Across the evaluated few-shot imitation policies, PrObe detects errors more effectively than strong baselines. Ablation experiments examine the contribution of its architectural choices, while a pilot error-correction study explores the practical usefulness of the task. The findings support adaptable monitoring as a way to identify deviations from demonstrated intent before an operator has access to a completed execution.
neurips-2024-aed-adaptable-error-detecti.tldr: PrObe detects behavior errors in few-shot imitation policies using visual observations and learned patterns that transfer to new environments.

paragraphs: When users edit an assistant's writing, their changes can reveal preferences as well as correct mistakes. PRELUDE treats this naturally occurring feedback as a source of personalization. It learns a written description of the user's preferences and uses that description to guide future prompts, avoiding model fine-tuning and allowing users to inspect or modify what was learned.

The proposed CIPHER algorithm accounts for preferences that depend on context. An LLM infers preferences from past edits, then retrieves those associated with the closest historical contexts when generating a new response. It combines the retrieved preferences into guidance for the current request. This makes the learned preference description an intermediate step between raw editing history and future output.

Evaluation covers summarization and email writing with a GPT-4 simulated user. CIPHER achieves the lowest edit-distance cost against methods that retrieve edits directly or learn preferences without accounting for context. Its preference descriptions also shorten prompts relative to direct edit retrieval, reducing computational expense. Further analysis finds substantial similarity between inferred preferences and the simulated user's underlying preferences.
neurips-2024-aligning-llm-agents-by-lear.tldr: CIPHER learns context-dependent preference descriptions from user edits and reduces subsequent editing in simulated writing tasks.

paragraphs: Autonomous driving combines understanding the current scene, predicting what will happen, and choosing a trajectory. These capabilities also need to operate within energy constraints. The paper introduces Spiking Autonomous Driving, or SAD, as a unified system that applies the event-driven, energy-efficient nature of spiking neural networks across this connected set of tasks.

SAD is trained end to end and contains three modules. Perception combines multiple camera views into a bird's-eye representation that captures spatial and temporal information. Prediction uses a dual-pathway design with spiking neurons to forecast future states. Planning then generates trajectories while considering predicted occupancy, traffic rules, and passenger comfort, connecting the forecasts to the vehicle's intended movement.

On the nuScenes dataset, SAD achieves competitive results across perception, prediction, and planning while drawing on the energy efficiency of spiking networks. The stated significance is the potential for neuromorphic computing to support an integrated driving system. The evidence concerns the evaluated tasks and establishes a promising direction for energy-efficient autonomous driving.
neurips-2024-autonomous-driving-with-spi.tldr: SAD combines perception, prediction, and planning in an end-to-end spiking neural network with competitive nuScenes performance.

paragraphs: DenseFormer changes how information moves through a transformer. After each transformer block, it adds a learned weighted average of the current representation and representations from earlier blocks. The operation, called Depth-Weighted-Average, gives later processing stages an explicit way to reuse information produced at multiple depths.

The modification adds very few parameters relative to the models discussed: only a few thousand for models around the hundred-billion-parameter scale. The learned averaging weights also reveal structured patterns, including substantial reuse of activations from distant layers. This matters because the additional connections are used in a coherent way, providing evidence that the model benefits from access to earlier representations.

Experiments report improved perplexity and greater data efficiency, with DenseFormer reaching the perplexity of substantially deeper transformers. When models are compared at the same perplexity, DenseFormer also improves memory efficiency and inference time over transformer baselines. The findings suggest that changing information flow across depth can improve predictive performance and computational efficiency without a substantial increase in parameter count.
neurips-2024-denseformer-enhancing-infor.tldr: DenseFormer learns weighted combinations of representations across transformer layers, improving perplexity and efficiency with very few additional parameters.

paragraphs: Learning from observation seeks to imitate an expert using demonstrations that show states without labeling the actions that produced them. Existing adversarial approaches train a policy to generate state transitions that a discriminator cannot distinguish from expert transitions. Although this setup is straightforward to describe, the paper identifies sensitivity to hyperparameters and brittle training as problems.

Diffusion Imitation from Observation, or DIFO, brings a diffusion model into that framework. The model learns about expert and agent transitions by generating a next state conditioned on the current state. The authors then reformulate its training objective so it acts as a binary classifier, providing rewards that indicate how expert-like the policy's transitions appear.

These rewards guide policy learning using the state-only demonstrations. The diffusion model therefore connects transition modeling with the feedback used to improve behavior. Experiments report superior performance across continuous-control settings covering navigation, locomotion, manipulation, and games. The results support this use of diffusion modeling as a component of imitation from observation across the tested domains.
neurips-2024-diffusion-imitation-from-ob.tldr: DIFO uses a diffusion-based transition classifier to reward expert-like behavior when learning from demonstrations without action labels.

paragraphs: How quickly a neural network learns depends on both its training rule and the structure of its data. Earlier perceptron theories often used student-teacher assumptions or simplified the output to a linear form. Those choices helped make analysis possible but restricted what the theories could explain about nonlinear responses and input distributions.

This paper uses a stochastic-process approach to derive equations describing how learning evolves in a nonlinear perceptron performing binary classification. The framework examines supervised and reinforcement learning, following both improvement on a task and the loss of that knowledge as subsequent tasks are learned. It therefore connects learning and forgetting within the same theoretical treatment.

The analysis finds that input noise affects learning speed differently under the two learning rules. It also influences how quickly later learning overwrites an earlier task. Verification using MNIST connects the approach to real data. The work provides a route toward analyzing more complex neural circuits, with its demonstrated analysis centered on the nonlinear perceptron.
neurips-2024-dynamics-of-supervised-and-.tldr: A stochastic-process theory explains how learning rules and input noise shape learning and forgetting in a nonlinear perceptron.

paragraphs: Financial investment decisions unfold over time, requiring repeated interpretation of information and adjustment to a volatile environment. FinCon organizes LLM agents around this problem using a manager-analyst hierarchy inspired by investment firms. Agents communicate in natural language and coordinate their different responsibilities toward shared objectives, helping combine information from multiple sources.

A risk-control component periodically triggers self-critique. The system uses that reflection to update its investment beliefs, expressing lessons as concepts that can guide later behavior. These verbal updates can be sent selectively to the agents that need them. This makes experience refinement part of the decision process while reducing unnecessary communication among peers.

The paper reports that this mechanism improves performance and that FinCon generalizes across financial tasks, including stock trading and portfolio management. Its central contribution is the combination of hierarchical collaboration and targeted revision of investment beliefs. The stated results support using structured communication and experience-based language feedback to improve sequential decision-making within the evaluated financial applications.
neurips-2024-fincon-a-synthesized-llm-mu.tldr: FinCon coordinates financial LLM agents through a manager-analyst hierarchy and targeted belief updates derived from periodic self-critique.

paragraphs: Urban data changes over time, comes from multiple sources, and can be unevenly distributed. Models trained for one task under an assumption that training and testing distributions match can struggle with new conditions. CMuST addresses this by learning across multiple spatiotemporal tasks while explicitly representing connections among different dimensions of urban data.

Its interaction network models relationships between contextual information and main observations, alongside interactions within spatial and temporal dimensions. This supports learning patterns shared across tasks while retaining task-specific characteristics. A Rolling Adaptation training scheme then enables continued learning: prompts derived from data summaries represent individual tasks, while iterative modeling of model behavior captures relationships among tasks.

The authors introduce a three-city benchmark and report improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods in extensive evaluations. These include settings with few-shot streaming data and tasks from new domains. The results support the idea that urban prediction benefits from jointly learning shared structure and task individuality, with continued adaptation providing a way to use that structure as new data and tasks arrive.
neurips-2024-get-rid-of-isolation-a-cont.tldr: CMuST combines cross-task spatiotemporal interactions with rolling adaptation to improve learning from streaming urban data and new domains.

paragraphs: Federated learning can overfit when individual clients have little data, producing predictions that are too confident. Representing uncertainty through posterior inference can help, but differences between clients' data can bias local posteriors and weaken the combined global result. FedMDMI addresses this tension through a global model-data mutual-information regularizer.

The regularizer is intended to help the global model learn essential information from heterogeneous client data. To make the objective manageable, the authors decompose the global information term into locally optimizable terms. They show that each resulting optimal local posterior has a Gibbs form and can be sampled using stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. The server approximates global posterior sampling by averaging local posterior samples.

The theoretical analysis provides a generalization bound expressed through model-data mutual information. Changing the regularization level yields a federated version of the bias-variance trade-off. Experiments report improved generalization and better-calibrated uncertainty estimates. Together, these findings connect an information-based training objective with both predictive performance and the reliability of the model's expressed uncertainty.
neurips-2024-improving-generalization-in.tldr: FedMDMI regularizes federated posterior inference with model-data mutual information to improve generalization and uncertainty calibration.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasters often predict from a fixed window of past observations. That can restrict access to longer patterns, while shuffling consecutive training samples into batches can discard useful relationships between them. The paper introduces Spectral Attention to preserve those relationships and bring longer-range information into models that still use fixed-size input windows.

The mechanism uses a low-pass filter to retain long-period trends and allows gradients to flow between samples. This links the treatment of slowly changing patterns with learning across temporally related examples. Spectral Attention preserves the base model's structure and is designed to integrate into most sequence models, enabling fixed-window forecasters to capture dependencies spanning thousands of steps.

Experiments apply the mechanism to seven recent forecasting models across eleven real-world time-series datasets. The authors report consistent effectiveness and state-of-the-art results. These findings support supplementing the information available within each input window by preserving temporal connections across samples, providing a way to address long-range forecasting without redesigning the underlying forecasting model.
neurips-2024-introducing-spectral-attent.tldr: Spectral Attention preserves long-period trends and links training samples so fixed-window forecasters can use longer-range information.

paragraphs: People can group elements into an object because they move together, a perceptual principle called common fate. This ability extends to unfamiliar textures and random dots without additional training. The paper investigates the computational basis of that generalization by testing whether motion-processing models can separate figures from backgrounds in random-dot videos.

The comparison includes forty deep optical-flow models trained on different datasets and a neuroscience-inspired motion-energy model fitted to recordings from cortical area MT. The optical-flow models struggle to recover motion patterns in these videos, leading to poor segmentation. The motion-energy model performs substantially better than all of the evaluated optical-flow models on the task.

A psychophysical study provides a comparison with people, using shape identification as a proxy for segmentation performance. The evaluated state-of-the-art optical-flow models fall below human performance, while the motion-energy model matches human capability. These results connect a model of cortical motion processing with human-like generalization in random-dot segmentation, offering a computational account of this specific common-fate ability.
neurips-2024-object-segmentation-from-co.tldr: A neuroscience-inspired motion-energy model matches human performance on random-dot segmentation where tested deep optical-flow models struggle.

paragraphs: Customized text-to-image diffusion models can learn from personal images, raising concerns about privacy and unauthorized artistic imitation. One protective approach changes those images with adversarial perturbations that interfere with their use by the model. Existing methods often tailor these changes to particular prompts, making their protection less adaptable when the textual request changes.

Prompt-Agnostic Adversarial Perturbation, or PAP, explicitly accounts for variation across prompts. It first models a prompt distribution using a Laplace approximation. It then searches for perturbations that maximize the expected disturbance under that modeled distribution. The protective objective therefore considers a distribution of possible prompts when determining how to alter an image.

Experiments cover face privacy and artistic-style protection. The authors report stronger generalization than existing techniques and improved stability of the defense. The findings support optimizing protection across prompt variation, because the effectiveness of an image perturbation depends on the requests used with a customized model. The reported advantage concerns generalization across the evaluated prompt and protection settings.
neurips-2024-prompt-agnostic-adversarial.tldr: PAP optimizes protective image perturbations over a modeled prompt distribution, improving generalization in face-privacy and artistic-style experiments.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines labeled examples with unlabeled data, which is useful when obtaining labels is difficult. Many methods rely on predefined rules for creating pseudo-labels or deciding how unlabeled examples should affect training. This paper introduces RLGSSL, which uses a reinforcement-learning formulation to guide the prediction model's learning process adaptively.

RLGSSL casts the problem as a one-armed bandit and introduces a training loss based on weighted reward. Its reward function is designed to balance information from labeled and unlabeled data in support of generalization. A semi-supervised teacher-student framework provides additional learning stability, bringing together reward-based guidance and a structure intended to make training more reliable.

Across several benchmark datasets, the authors report consistently better performance than state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods. The contribution is an alternative way to determine how the available supervision and unlabeled data shape model training. The stated findings indicate that the proposed reward-guided objective and stabilizing framework work effectively together in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-reinforcement-learning-guid.tldr: RLGSSL uses a weighted reinforcement-learning reward and a teacher-student framework to guide learning from labeled and unlabeled data.

paragraphs: Data curation determines which examples become a training dataset, making it a central part of learning. SELECT provides a large-scale benchmark for systematically comparing curation strategies in image classification. To support it, the authors create ImageNet++, extending ImageNet with five additional training-data distributions, each roughly the size of ImageNet-1K and assembled through a different strategy.

The benchmark examines these datasets in two ways. First, identical classification models are trained from scratch on each training-data distribution. Second, each distribution is used to inspect a fixed pretrained self-supervised representation. These evaluations provide distinct views of how the choice of training examples relates to learning and to an already learned representation.

The results show that synthetic data generation and retrieval through CLIP embeddings can be highly competitive for particular tasks. Nevertheless, the authors find that the curation strategy behind the original ImageNet-1K remains the strongest overall reference in their comparison. SELECT makes these differences measurable within a shared evaluation framework, helping identify where newer curation methods are effective and where a gap remains.
neurips-2024-select-a-large-scale-benchm.tldr: SELECT compares image-dataset curation strategies at scale and finds that newer methods compete on some tasks while original ImageNet curation remains the reference standard.

paragraphs: An ensemble combines several models, so its performance depends on both the properties of individual members and the differences between them. This paper studies the relationship between diversity and sharpness, which describes how sensitive a model's loss is around its learned parameters. Both have been linked to generalization, but improving them together presents a trade-off.

The authors find that reducing sharpness tends to reduce diversity among ensemble members. That loss of diversity can diminish the benefit of combining the models. They support this relationship through theoretical analysis and experiments, then introduce SharpBalance, a training approach designed to balance the two properties. Their theory shows that the strategy achieves a better sharpness-diversity trade-off.

Evaluations on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet report improvements in both the trade-off and ensemble performance. The gains cover data from the training distribution and data outside it. The findings show why optimizing individual models for flatter solutions can have consequences at the ensemble level, and support explicitly considering member diversity during training.
neurips-2024-sharpness-diversity-tradeof.tldr: SharpBalance improves ensembles by addressing the tendency for flatter individual models to become less diverse.

paragraphs: Data attribution estimates how individual training examples influence a model's predictions. Many methods address this question, but developing, integrating, and comparing them requires shared infrastructure. The paper introduces dattri, an open-source library designed to support those activities through a common interface and reusable computational components.

Its API allows different attribution methods to be incorporated into PyTorch pipelines with only a few lines changed. Lower-level utilities, including Hessian-vector products, inverse-Hessian-vector products, and random projections, are organized into reusable modules. These building blocks give researchers common implementations of operations used across attribution techniques, making it easier to develop new methods within the same framework.

The library also supplies pretrained models and ground-truth annotations for benchmarking, including generative AI settings. It implements multiple efficient attribution methods applicable to large neural networks. Using this infrastructure, the authors conduct a broad, fair comparison of attribution approaches. The contribution combines practical integration, method-development support, and evaluation resources so that different attribution methods can be studied within a consistent environment.
neurips-2024-texttt-dattri-a-library-for.tldr: dattri provides a unified PyTorch interface, reusable computations, and benchmarks for developing and comparing data-attribution methods.

paragraphs: Fairness metrics are often used to judge whether a predictive model treats groups fairly. Those judgments depend on the data and assumptions behind the evaluation. Measurement biases or other assumption violations can undermine what a fairness score means. This paper adapts causal sensitivity analysis to examine how robust fairness assessments are to such problems.

The framework accommodates effectively any combination of fairness metric and bias that can be expressed in the oblivious setting. It also examines multiple biases together, allowing their combined effect to be nonlinear. Researchers can encode domain-specific assumptions and constraints, making the analysis responsive to the kinds of data problems considered plausible in a particular application.

The authors study common parity metrics using three classifier varieties across fourteen fairness datasets. They find that even small dataset biases can make fairness assessments strikingly fragile. The contribution is a way to evaluate how informative a reported parity result remains when its underlying assumptions are questioned, providing context for interpreting the metric itself.
neurips-2024-the-fragility-of-fairness-c.tldr: Causal sensitivity analysis reveals that common fairness assessments can be highly fragile to small dataset biases.

paragraphs: Intervention planning in an opinion network involves choosing where to introduce accurate information and how to act as opinions evolve. Searching for effective plans becomes computationally difficult as networks grow. This paper studies learning-based approaches that identify influential intervention nodes and produce plans to reduce the spread of misinformation.

One approach ranks important nodes and uses those rankings to train neural-network classifiers for search and planning. A second uses centralized reinforcement learning to reduce the difficulty of generating training labels for larger networks. The authors evaluate planners under two opinion-propagation models, considering binary and continuous representations of opinions and trust.

Ranking-based classifiers improve infection-rate control especially in small networks with larger action budgets. Reward strategies emphasizing susceptible-node counts and infection rates outperform those emphasizing rapid blocking. Graph-convolutional planners also achieve lower infection rates across tested network configurations. These findings connect planning effectiveness to both the representation of network structure and the choice of reward, with the reported advantages varying across the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-towards-effective-planning-.tldr: Learned planners use node rankings and reinforcement learning to improve misinformation control across tested dynamic opinion networks.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can produce high-quality samples, but training them successfully typically requires substantial data. When a target domain has few examples, transferring knowledge from an existing model becomes valuable. This paper proposes the Transfer Guided Diffusion Process, or TGDP, as a different approach from conventional fine-tuning and regularization-based transfer.

The authors prove a relationship in which the optimal target-domain diffusion model combines pretrained source-domain diffusion models with guidance from a domain classifier. That result provides the basis for the proposed transfer process. The classifier supplies domain-related guidance, while the pretrained models contribute knowledge already learned from source data.

The paper also develops a conditional version that models data together with its labels and adds two regularization terms to improve performance. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of TGDP. The contribution connects a theoretical characterization of the target model with a practical transfer method, offering a way to use source-domain generative knowledge when target-domain training data is limited.
neurips-2024-transfer-learning-for-diffu.tldr: TGDP transfers diffusion models through domain-classifier guidance, supported by a theoretical characterization of the optimal target-domain model.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models route each token to a subset of their experts, leaving others unused for that token. Activating additional experts might appear to offer an easy improvement, but the paper's exploratory studies show that it does not necessarily help and can reduce output quality. Different routing strategies also produce substantially different output distributions.

SCMoE uses these differences through self-contrast during inference. It determines next-token probabilities by contrasting outputs from strong and weak activation within the same model, giving unchosen experts a role in generation. The method requires no training, and the authors report minimal added latency compared with greedy decoding.

Experiments with Mixtral 8x7B show consistent reasoning improvements across GSM8K, StrategyQA, MBPP, and HumanEval. GSM8K accuracy rises from 61.79 to 66.94, while combining the method with self-consistency raises major@20 accuracy from 75.59 to 78.31. The results support using differences between expert activation patterns as useful inference-time information, with additional gains possible when combined with self-consistency.
neurips-2024-unchosen-experts-can-contri.tldr: SCMoE improves tested MoE reasoning by contrasting strong and weak expert activations during inference without additional training.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary part segmentation identifies fine-grained entities in images using varied vocabulary, including terms not previously seen. The challenge extends beyond drawing precise boundaries: parts can be described at different levels of detail, and recognizing them depends on knowledge about what belongs to an object. The paper examines these issues through a framework called PartCLIPSeg.

PartCLIPSeg uses generalized parts together with object-level context to improve generalization to fine-grained parts. It also incorporates competitive relationships among parts and attention control. These mechanisms address ambiguous boundaries and parts that are underrepresented, connecting the interpretation of individual regions with information about other parts and the containing object.

Experiments on Pascal-Part-116, ADE20K-Part-234, and PartImageNet report significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods. The results include more refined segmentation and better handling of relationships between parts. The stated contribution is an approach that treats part identification as a problem involving context, relationships, and levels of granularity, bringing those sources of information together in open-vocabulary segmentation.
neurips-2024-understanding-multi-granula.tldr: PartCLIPSeg uses object context, generalized parts, and relationships among parts to improve open-vocabulary part segmentation.

paragraphs: Many datasets contain geometric structure or symmetries that neural networks can incorporate into their design. Group convolutions provide one way to do this, but deeper architectures can become unstable and struggle with long-range dependencies. In graph networks, repeated message passing can make node representations converge toward one another, a problem known as over-smoothing.

The paper proposes unitary group convolutions to support deeper networks with more stable training. Its main focus is graph learning, where the authors prove that unitary graph convolutions avoid over-smoothing. This directly addresses the loss of distinction among node representations that can otherwise appear after only a few rounds of message passing.

Experiments show competitive performance against state-of-the-art graph neural networks on benchmark datasets. The paper also studies unitary convolutions beyond graphs and analyzes their role in stabilizing general group-convolutional architectures. Its contribution combines a specific theoretical protection against graph over-smoothing with empirical evidence that the resulting networks remain useful on benchmark tasks.
neurips-2024-unitary-convolutions-for-le.tldr: Unitary graph convolutions provably avoid over-smoothing and achieve competitive benchmark performance while supporting more stable deep networks.

paragraphs: Pretrained vision-language object detectors can generalize to categories or settings without task-specific training. Adapting them sequentially to specialized domains introduces a second objective: preserving that broad zero-shot ability while learning new tasks. This paper formalizes the combined challenge as Incremental Vision-Language Object Detection.

The proposed method, ZiRa, combines a Zero-interference Loss with reparameterization techniques. It is designed to support incremental adaptation without a significant increase in memory usage. The goal brings specialized-domain learning and general-domain retention into the same adaptation procedure, so progress on new tasks is evaluated alongside continued zero-shot capability.

Experiments on COCO and ODinW-13 show that ZiRa preserves zero-shot generalization while adapting continuously to new tasks. After training on ODinW-13, its zero-shot performance exceeds CL-DETR by 13.91 AP and iDETR by 8.74 AP. These findings demonstrate the method's effectiveness on the proposed combined objective in the tested settings, highlighting the value of explicitly protecting generalization during sequential specialization.
neurips-2024-zero-shot-generalizable-inc.tldr: ZiRa adapts vision-language object detectors to successive specialized tasks while preserving zero-shot generalization with little additional memory.
